newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea finmin details medium-term reforms.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea finmin details medium-term reforms.

text.p: South Korea's Finance Ministry on Wednesday revealed more details of its plan for medium-term financial reforms.

A ministry statement said the government would generally accept draft proposals of the Presidential Commission for Financial Reform, which recommended more transparent rules for new entrants into the financial industry and lower minimum capital requirements for some financial institutions.
Under the plan, the unified financial watchdog of banks, securities and insurers is required to inform an applicant of its entry within three months after application.
The statement said the ministry would keep the current minimum capital requirement for city banks and regional banks at 100 billion won and 30 billion won respectively.
It was also considering lowering the requirement for entering the brokerage business from the commission's proposed 10 billion won.
South Korea is expected to introduce a bridge bank to handle possible bankruptcies by banks.

The statement said the ministry would accept the commission's recommendation for a system in which financial institutions would be classified into several categories in accordance with their equity capital-to-asset ratio.

South Korea's top 30 business conglomerates or chaebols would be required to submit consolidated financial statements, including balance sheets and profit and loss statements for all affiliates, from the calendar year 2000.

The ministry would also reinforce rules requiring corporates to report information to the Korea Stock Exchange and come up with measures to encourage collective lawsuits to protect small investors' rights.

In a departure from the commission's recommendation, the ministry would push forward with its original plan to allow the top five chaebols to enter the life insurance business from 2003. The commission had proposed 2000 as the first year, but the statement said the industry would need more time to restructure.
The ministry said it would study further proposals to require submission of quarterly financial reports by listed companies and to help finance the merger of financial institutions.
Legislation implementing the finance ministry's plans needs approval from the National Assembly.
Analysts say a special parliamentary session in July was unlikely to pass the reform bill because of criticism from financial institutions and lawmakers' focus on the December presidential election.
